33:53.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ لَا تَدۡخُلُواْ بُيُوتَ ٱلنَّبِيِّ إِلَّآ أَن يُؤۡذَنَ لَكُمۡ إِلَىٰ طَعَامٍ غَيۡرَ نَٰظِرِينَ إِنَىٰهُ وَلَٰكِنۡ إِذَا دُعِيتُمۡ فَٱدۡخُلُواْ فَإِذَا طَعِمۡتُمۡ فَٱنتَشِرُواْ وَلَا مُسۡتَـٔۡنِسِينَ لِحَدِيثٍۚ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكُمۡ كَانَ يُؤۡذِي ٱلنَّبِيَّ فَيَسۡتَحۡيِۦ مِنكُمۡۖ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يَسۡتَحۡيِۦ مِنَ ٱلۡحَقِّۚ وَإِذَا سَأَلۡتُمُوهُنَّ مَتَٰعࣰ ا فَسۡـَٔلُوهُنَّ مِن وَرَآءِ حِجَابࣲۚ ذَٰلِكُمۡ أَطۡهَرُ لِقُلُوبِكُمۡ وَقُلُوبِهِنَّۚ وَمَا كَانَ لَكُمۡ أَن تُؤۡذُواْ رَسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَلَآ أَن تَنكِحُوٓاْ أَزۡوَٰجَهُۥ مِنۢ بَعۡدِهِۦٓ أَبَدًاۚ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكُمۡ كَانَ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ عَظِيمًا
33:53.en: O you who have believed, do not enter the houses of the Prophet except when you are permitted for a meal, without awaiting its readiness. But when you are invited, then enter; and when you have eaten, disperse without seeking to remain for conversation. Indeed, that [behavior] was troubling the Prophet, and he is shy of [dismissing] you. But Allah is not shy of the truth. And when you ask [his wives] for something, ask them from behind a partition. That is purer for your hearts and their hearts. And it is not [conceivable or lawful] for you to harm the Messenger of Allah or to marry his wives after him, ever. Indeed, that would be in the sight of Allah an enormity

ofxBCOgeNj8.speaker: adnan
ofxBCOgeNj8.speaker_note: Continuation of his own Ramadan morning series on the Prophet's attributes
ofxBCOgeNj8.title: Attributes of the Prophet: His Physical Description
ofxBCOgeNj8.one_line: What the companions said the Prophet looked like, from Hind ibn Abi Halah's detailed portrait to Ali's short summary of his character.
ofxBCOgeNj8.summary: He argues that a Muslim who does not know the Prophet will struggle to follow his law for a lifetime, so knowing him, including how he looked, matters. He notes that senior companions rarely stared at his face out of reverence, so the detailed descriptions come from those who were children around him. He moves through the narrations: Jabir comparing his face to the full moon, Aisha on his glowing sweat, and at length the description that Hind ibn Abi Halah gave to his nephew al-Hasan, who grieved that he could no longer remember his grandfather's face. From it he draws the Prophet's innate dignity, height, hair, brow, teeth, hands, feet and build, adding light asides such as going easy on sons over hairstyles. He then turns to manner: lowered gaze, greeting first, few but precise words, never belittling a blessing, angry only when truth was violated, and the wrestling match with Rukanah. He closes with his favourite description, from Ali: the most generous heart, someone who never made you feel a burden and raised you higher the longer you stayed with him; at first sight you revered him, and on knowing him you loved him. The aim is that learning his description deepens love and following.

outline.heading: Knowing the Prophet as the basis for following him
outline.gist: Nothing is more beneficial than learning about him; a Muslim who does not know and love his Prophet will find it hard to keep his law for life.

outline.heading: Why the descriptions come from the younger companions
outline.gist: Older companions lowered their gaze out of respect, so detailed portraits come from those who sat near him as children.

outline.heading: Jabir and the full moon
outline.gist: Comparing his face to the full moon, he found the Prophet more beautiful; love also makes the beloved's face beautiful. Aisha said even his sweat glowed.

outline.heading: Aisha and the misplaced line of poetry
outline.gist: Aisha told him a famous verse about a face lighting up like lightning was really about him, hours before his death.

outline.heading: Al-Hasan asks his uncle Hind ibn Abi Halah
outline.gist: He accepts a study grading the long narration as sound, and explains who Hind was: Khadijah's son, raised in the Prophet's house.

outline.heading: The grief of forgetting a loved one's face
outline.gist: Al-Hasan, orphaned of his grandfather as a child, could not recall his face and asked to hear it described again.

outline.heading: Innate dignity and a face like the full moon
outline.gist: He was naturally imposing and refined, independent of clothing or money, and his face shone like the full moon.

outline.heading: Height and hair
outline.gist: Slightly above average height, hair between curly and straight, often long and sometimes braided; parents should go easy on their sons over hair.

outline.heading: Brow, forehead and teeth
outline.gist: Fine full eyebrows with a vein between them that showed when he was angry, a broad forehead, wide mouth and small gaps beside the front teeth.

outline.heading: Hands, feet and build
outline.gist: Little body hair, large joints, long tapering fingers, arched feet, light skin under his clothes and a firm, muscled stomach.

outline.heading: Gaze, walk and greeting
outline.gist: He looked at the ground more than the sky, did not stare, let his companions walk ahead and always greeted first.

outline.heading: Wrestling Rukanah
outline.gist: A champion wrestler who would only listen to strength challenged him; the Prophet threw him repeatedly.

outline.heading: His inner state and speech
outline.gist: Continually grieved and thoughtful, yet always smiling; he spoke little but precisely, was easygoing but not a pushover, and magnified every blessing.

outline.heading: Gestures and smile
outline.gist: He gestured with the whole hand, turned fully to whoever he spoke with, and his laughter was mostly a broad smile.

outline.heading: Umm Sulaym collects his sweat
outline.gist: She gathered his sweat for its fragrance and blessing; his hand was the softest anyone touched and smelled of musk.

outline.heading: Ali's description: the most generous heart
outline.gist: He gave time and wealth without making anyone feel a burden, even guests who overstayed in his home, as the Quran later addressed.

outline.heading: The longer you stayed, the higher he raised you
outline.gist: He never took people for granted or set them aside for newcomers, and nothing was a big deal to him.

outline.heading: Angry only for the truth; reverence then love
outline.gist: He never got angry for himself, only when someone oppressed or crossed Allah's limits. At first sight people revered him; knowing him, they loved him.

outline.heading: No one like him before or after
outline.gist: Those who saw him attest that no one was ever remotely like him in mercy, grit, bravery and generosity.

outline.heading: Outro

7:150.ar: وَلَمَّا رَجَعَ مُوسَىٰٓ إِلَىٰ قَوۡمِهِۦ غَضۡبَٰنَ أَسِفࣰ ا قَالَ بِئۡسَمَا خَلَفۡتُمُونِي مِنۢ بَعۡدِيٓۖ أَعَجِلۡتُمۡ أَمۡرَ رَبِّكُمۡۖ وَأَلۡقَى ٱلۡأَلۡوَاحَ وَأَخَذَ بِرَأۡسِ أَخِيهِ يَجُرُّهُۥٓ إِلَيۡهِۚ قَالَ ٱبۡنَ أُمَّ إِنَّ ٱلۡقَوۡمَ ٱسۡتَضۡعَفُونِي وَكَادُواْ يَقۡتُلُونَنِي فَلَا تُشۡمِتۡ بِيَ ٱلۡأَعۡدَآءَ وَلَا تَجۡعَلۡنِي مَعَ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ

CZ5XigjEVCc.speaker: adnan
CZ5XigjEVCc.speaker_note: Final session of his own Ramadan series; speaks of his years in Syria and his community in London
CZ5XigjEVCc.title: Attributes of the Prophet: Our Following of the Prophet
CZ5XigjEVCc.one_line: Closing the series: Ramadan must bear fruit in following the Prophet, serving his ummah, and five areas the community must invest in.
CZ5XigjEVCc.summary: Closing his Ramadan series on the Prophet's attributes, he argues that worship must produce a visible fruit; otherwise the effort disperses into nothing. The first fruit is following the Prophet honestly, holding ourselves to his standard and learning to think as he thought. The companions used worship as fuel for building the ummah, as night prayer prepared the Prophet for a heavy message, so Ramadan is a beginning, a boot camp, not an end. Nothing should come ahead of Allah and His Messenger, and the believer's horizon must be the state of the Prophet's ummah, whose guidance benefits all people. We must be able to plead before Allah that we tried, like Shuayb seeking reform as far as he could, without judging who will accept. Reflecting on ten years since leaving Syria, he says one belongs by serving and must work wherever Allah has placed him, asking whether anyone benefits from his existence. He proposes five areas for the community: education, outreach to Muslims and non-Muslims, mentorship, financial organisation, and advocacy. He ends with Musa, Yunus and Uthman to show that one big, sincere contribution outweighs small faults, and urges listeners to make Ramadan the start of their story.

outline.heading: Opening
Looking back on the attributes covered
outline.gist: He lists the traits and relationships of the Prophet the series covered, and turns now to our following of him.

outline.heading: Every act of worship must bear fruit
outline.gist: After a month of effort something in character, habits and routine must change, or the energy is lost; ask what the fruit of your worship is.

outline.heading: Follow him to his standard, and think as he thought
outline.gist: The best among us is the one who follows him most; we must imitate not only his behaviour but his way of thinking, and measure ourselves a step closer.

outline.heading: Worship as fuel: night prayer before a heavy word
outline.gist: The companions used worship to power their work for the ummah, just as Allah told the Prophet to pray at night before giving him a heavy message to carry.

outline.heading: Ramadan is a beginning, a boot camp
outline.gist: Things begin with Ramadan; it recentres, trains and strengthens us so we can do the job afterwards.

outline.heading: Nothing ahead of Allah and His Messenger
outline.gist: He is the excellent model for those who seek Allah and the Hereafter; nothing in our priorities comes before them.

outline.heading: Take what he gave you; follow him to be loved
outline.gist: Embrace what he brought and avoid what he forbade; following him is how love of Allah is proven.

outline.heading: The state of his ummah as the goal
outline.gist: Beyond work and the masjid, believers need a long-term vision of the ummah rising again, identifying its gaps and fixing them.

outline.heading: The best nation for all people
outline.gist: The good of this world comes through this ummah's guidance, which serves believers and non-believers alike; like children, people do not always know what is good for them.

outline.heading: An excuse before your Lord
outline.gist: Many Muslims lack concern beyond themselves; like those in the Quran who kept advising a doomed town, we must be able to plead before Allah that we tried.

outline.heading: You do not know who will accept
outline.gist: The masjid never planned for converts yet dozens embraced Islam in a year, mostly brought by young friends; just do your part.

outline.heading: Shuayb: reform as far as I am able
outline.gist: His favourite verse: the aim is reform to the limit of one's capacity.

outline.heading: Belonging by serving
outline.gist: Never fully accepted in Canada, Saudi or Syria, he was told by a teacher that the only way to belong is to serve, and spent fifteen years serving youth in Syria until he was accepted.

outline.heading: Uprooted, and still seeking fruit
outline.gist: Forced to leave after detention, he found measuring progress hard in a new land without degree, network or vocabulary, but ten idle years would be ten wasted years.

outline.heading: Work where Allah put you
outline.gist: Circumstances are never optimal; ask whether anyone benefits from your being alive and push something forward, however small.

outline.heading: Time flies; a bigger goal makes it bearable
outline.gist: Ten years pass in a blink and midlife crises come from refusing that; a goal beyond degree, marriage and house makes the passing of time meaningful.

outline.heading: Community priority: education
outline.gist: Islamic and broader education, skills and the right knowledge at the right life stage, with lifelong learning and narratives youth can defend.

outline.heading: Community priority: outreach
outline.gist: Dawah to Muslims in the grey area who feel unwelcome in masjids, and to non-Muslims, which is the reason for living here.

outline.heading: Community priority: mentorship
outline.gist: Distinct from education: role models who help youth build identity and belonging; university students and professionals must give time, as mentors saved him.

outline.heading: Community priority: financial organisation
outline.gist: The community has wealth but poor management and no centralisation, relying on constant fundraising while masjid budgets lag far behind other faiths.

outline.heading: Community priority: advocacy
outline.gist: Laws should reflect the will of a million Canadian Muslims; the generation born here must reject the keep-your-head-down mentality and organise.

outline.heading: Education and mentorship are not the same
outline.gist: Education needs people of knowledge; mentorship needs decent people willing to give time.

outline.heading: What the Prophet would tell us
outline.gist: The five areas came from asking what he would advise: invest in people and community, with the global ummah as the bigger goal.

outline.heading: Make Ramadan the beginning of your story
outline.gist: Dream big and bring something great to Allah, who could scrutinise every moment but overlooks much for a great deed.

outline.heading: Musa's anger overlooked; Yunus's departure
outline.gist: Musa's throwing of the tablets drew no rebuke because of his stand before Pharaoh despite fear, while Yunus left his people without permission and was tested in the whale.

outline.heading: Uthman: nothing will harm him after today
outline.gist: Uthman equipped an army and bought a well for Madinah; one great deed at the right moment covers later mistakes.

outline.heading: Outro
